messages.subject: Models for distance in R
parts:
Hello it is me again, 

I was plotting my models with their adjustments for my dataset. Now i have run into the problem that every model i generate for one specific dataset has a significant Cramer von misses. I have tried to change the truncation but this had no effect and the models kept not being a good fit. 

No truncation, 5% truncation and 10% truncation of my dataset with models halfnormal cosine and hermite, uniform cosine and hazard rate polynomial all have Cramer von misses <0.05. 

An example code for one of my models with 5% truncation is: 
TD2WPTotal.hn.cos <- ds(data = TD2WPTotal, key="hn", adjustment="cos", truncation = 43.4, convert_units = conversion.factor)
and the plot() with the model below (plot(TD2WPTotal.hn.cos, breaks=cutpoints1))

and the goodness of fit test gives:
> gof_ds(TD2WPTotal.hn.cos) Goodness of fit results for ddf object Distance sampling Cramer-von Mises test (unweighted) Test statistic = 0.698234 p-value = 0.0128639


Is there another way to make changes in my dataset so that i get models that do fit my dataset? 

With kind regards, 

Casolyn

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Models for distance in R
parts:
Casolyn

Looks like you are making good progress with your investigation. The histogram and QQ plot you provide are enlightening. The QQ plot specifically shows that the predominant lack of fit is at small distances. You might also plot your histogram of observed distances with many more distance bins—it appears that you have a large number of detections, so a more fine-grained histogram might show the source of the fit problems (although plots do not fix the problems). If the lack of fit is at small distances, truncation (removing detections at large distances) will have no effect upon fit.

"Spikes" in the histogram at small distances are notoriously difficult to deal with. Such data can arise from rounding perpendicular distances to 0 or observers trying to "guard" the transect by devoting too much effort to watching the transect. There is little to be done about this at the analysis stage.

You may need to make inference from a detection function that fails to adequately fit the data. You will need to note this threat to your inference in the report you produce.
